--- title: "[Graph.alpha_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get alpha centrality for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L26770-L26933){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.alpha_centrality( alpha=0.1, max_iter=100, tol=1e-06, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Alpha centrality](/assets/graphs/alpha-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same five-node directed graph shaded by alpha centrality with alpha 0.8, which follows outgoing edges. The source A, whose arcs reach every other node, scores 0.45, then B and C 0.17, D 0.13, and the sink E, which reaches nothing, only its exogenous share, 0.07." width="100%"} Alpha centrality is a generalization of eigenvector centrality that adds an exogenous factor: `x = α · A · x + e` where `α` is the attenuation factor, `A` is the adjacency matrix, and `e` is the exogenous factor (set to `1` for all nodes). Lower `α` emphasizes local neighborhood structure, while higher `α` considers more global structure. The returned scores are the fixed point of this equation, scaled to sum to `1`. The iteration converges only when `α` is below `1 / λ_max`, the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of `A`. Equivalently, a node's score counts the walks that *start* at it, with a walk of length `k` weighted by `α^k`. Every node gets a baseline of `1` from `e`, so, unlike plain eigenvector centrality, nodes outside strongly connected cores (including every node of an acyclic graph) still receive meaningful, non-zero scores. This makes alpha centrality a good choice for: - directed acyclic networks such as dependency, citation, or supply-chain graphs, where eigenvector centrality degenerates - measuring how much of the network a node can reach and influence through its outgoing edges - interpolating between degree-like (small `α`) and eigenvector-like (large `α`) rankings In a directed graph the sum runs over each node's successors, so the score reflects outgoing reach (see `katz_centrality()` for the incoming-edge counterpart). Edge weights are ignored. The fixed point is found by simple iteration starting from all-ones; if `α` is at or above `1 / λ_max` the values grow without bound; the method then emits a `RuntimeWarning` after `max_iter=` rounds (or as soon as the values overflow), and the returned scores are meaningless, so check `α` against the graph's spectrum when using large values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [alpha]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.1]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Attenuation factor applied to each additional step of a walk. Defaults to `0.1`. Must be positive and below `1 / λ_max` for the iteration to converge (for an undirected graph `λ_max` is at least the average degree and at most the maximum degree; for a directed acyclic graph it is `0`, so any value works). Small values make the ranking close to (out-)degree; values approaching `1 / λ_max` make it approach eigenvector centrality. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of iterations. Defaults to `100`. If the scores have not converged by then, the values from the last iteration are normalized and returned without a warning. Convergence slows as `alpha=` approaches `1 / λ_max`, so increase this when using large `alpha=` values. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence threshold. Iteration stops once the largest relative change of any node's (unnormalized) score between two iterations falls below `tol=`. Defaults to `1e-6`. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"alpha_centrality"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. Only used when `return_dict=` is `False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the scores as a dictionary and leave the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), store the scores under `attr_name=` and return the graph for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to centrality scores, which sum to `1`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Lower `alpha=` values keep the focus on a node's immediate neighborhood, while higher values let influence propagate further through the network. On a star graph (`λ_max = sqrt(3)`, so `alpha=` must stay below about `0.577`), raising `alpha=` from `0.05` to `0.5` increases the hub's share from about `0.27` to about `0.36`: ::: {#23d6bd87 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["hub", "A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("hub", "A"), ("hub", "B"), ("hub", "C")]) ) low = graph.alpha_centrality(alpha=0.05, return_dict=True) high = graph.alpha_centrality(alpha=0.5, return_dict=True) { graph.get_label_from_id(nid): (round(low[nid], 3), round(high[nid], 3)) for nid in sorted(low) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'hub': (0.267, 0.357), 'A': (0.244, 0.214), 'B': (0.244, 0.214), 'C': (0.244, 0.214)} ``` ::: ::: Alpha centrality works on directed acyclic graphs, where eigenvector centrality breaks down. Here A points to B, C, and D; B and C point to D; and D points to E. Scores follow outgoing edges, so A, which can reach every other node, ranks first and the sink E, which reaches nothing, keeps only its baseline share: ::: {#f2a10b38 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} dag = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) ) scores = dag.alpha_centrality(alpha=0.8, return_dict=True) {dag.get_label_from_id(nid): round(s, 3) for nid, s in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'A': 0.452, 'B': 0.174, 'C': 0.174, 'D': 0.128, 'E': 0.071} ``` ::: ::: Storing the result as a node attribute lets it chain directly into visualization methods like `colorize_node_attrs()`: ::: {#3a9b4584 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph .alpha_centrality(attr_name="alpha_cent") .colorize_node_attrs(node_attr_from="alpha_cent", node_attr_to="fillcolor") .get_node_df() .select(["label", "alpha_cent", "fillcolor"]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
